title: A Glasshouse for the Silence
premise: Mara Crane, a restaurant critic who lost her ability to taste after her family's death in a fire she survived, has built a career on elegant evasion—reviews full of atmosphere and never a single honest sentence about flavor. When she is sent to profile Ilse Vann, the last fluent speaker of Kessari, a dying language with no word for 'alone,' Ilse offers to teach her in exchange for one thing: Mara must eventually translate a sentence Ilse refuses to explain, using only words Mara truly means. As Ilse's health fails, Mara discovers the sentence is a confession Ilse has carried since the war, and translating it forces Mara to finally speak her own unsaid truth about the night of the fire. The book ends with Ilse's death and Mara publishing a review that is simply the translated sentence—her first honest sentence in seven years—signed not as a critic but as a student, finding belonging not in a family she lost but in the one she finally lets form around her grief.
about_author: Yara Coldharbour is the pen name of a former interpreter who spent a decade documenting endangered languages across three continents before turning to fiction. She lives in a coastal town with a deaf dog and a garden she describes as 'a negotiation, not a victory.'

chapters.title: The Review of Empty Rooms
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. We meet Mara mid-review, writing beautifully about a meal she cannot taste, her palate burned out since the fire that killed her parents and brother seven years ago. Assigned to profile Ilse Vann, the last speaker of Kessari, Mara arrives intending a quick, flattering piece. Ilse sees through her instantly, refusing to be written about 'by someone who has stopped saying things.' Emotional beat: recognition—the terror of being truly perceived.

chapters.title: Words That Refuse to Be Alone
chapters.summary: Alternating Mara and Ilse POV. Ilse agrees to teach Mara Kessari if she attends weekly, learns by cooking alongside her, and accepts one condition: at the end, Mara must translate a single sealed sentence Ilse wrote during the war. Mara's reviews begin to crack with accidental honesty; her editor notices. Emotional beat: cautious tenderness—found family forming through vocabulary, each woman teaching the other how to stay.

chapters.title: The Sentence in the Tin
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, with Ilse's voice entering through dictation as her strength fails. Ilse is hospitalized; Mara keeps the lessons alive at the bedside. She finally opens the tin: the sentence is Ilse's wartime confession of denouncing the man she loved to survive. Ilse asks not for forgiveness but for witness. Emotional beat: climax—Mara realizes translation requires meaning it, and to mean it she must finally say what she has never said about the fire: that she locked the door.

chapters.title: What Survives Translation
chapters.summary: Mara's POV, closing with Ilse's recorded voice. Ilse dies; at the funeral Mara meets the scattered students of Kessari's last decade—a found congregation of the almost-silent. She publishes her final review: no restaurant, just the translated sentence and her own confession beside it, signed as a student. The piece goes quietly viral among the grieving. Emotional beat: resolution—belonging as inheritance, silence finally spoken, taste returning in the last line as salt.
